name: Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
summary: The thinnest cranial nerve and the only one to emerge from the back of the brainstem and to cross before leaving: from the nucleus in the caudal midbrain the fibers curve dorsally around the aqueduct, decussate in the superior medullary velum and exit below the inferior colliculus to supply the contralateral superior oblique. Its long subarachnoid course around the midbrain and along the free edge of the tentorium makes it the nerve most often damaged by closed head injury. Palsy produces vertical diplopia worse looking down and in (reading, stairs) with a compensatory head tilt away from the affected eye.

anatomy.location: Nucleus in the periaqueductal gray at the inferior colliculus → fibers dorsally around the aqueduct, crossing in the superior medullary velum → exit on the dorsal midbrain below the inferior colliculus → around the cerebral peduncle in the ambient cistern beneath the free edge of the tentorium → lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below III → superior orbital fissure outside the annulus → superior oblique.

function: Depression of the adducted eye, intorsion of the abducted eye; keeps the eyes level during head tilt.

bestView.label: dorsal exit below the inferior colliculus
cisternal course around the midbrain beneath the tentorial edge
trochlear nerve in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below the third nerve

imaging.normalAppearance: Rarely visible on routine MRI; 3D CISS sometimes shows it in the ambient cistern. Imaging is often normal in isolated palsies; the yield rises with other signs. The BodyParts3D mesh in this atlas shows the orbital course.

pathology.finding: Usually normal; occasionally dorsal midbrain contusion or subarachnoid blood in the quadrigeminal cistern; often bilateral after severe trauma.
Small lesion of the caudal periaqueductal gray or superior medullary velum with a contralateral palsy.
Hypoplastic or absent nerve and small superior oblique on orbital MRI; long-standing head tilt in old photographs.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: MRI with thin brainstem and cavernous sinus sequences when the palsy is not traumatic or congenital

lesionEffects.deficit: Vertical (and torsional) diplopia worse on down-gaze and gaze to the opposite side
lesionEffects.mechanism: Superior oblique weakness: hypertropia of the affected eye

lesionEffects.deficit: Head tilt away from the affected eye, chin down
lesionEffects.mechanism: Compensation for the loss of intorsion and depression
Nuclear or fascicular lesion before the decussation

examination: Cover test for hypertropia in the nine positions
Parks–Bielschowsky three-step test: hypertropia increases on gaze to the opposite side and on head tilt to the same side
Look for a long-standing head tilt in photographs
Examine the other ocular motor nerves and the pupil
pearls: Diplopia going down stairs or reading with a head tilt is the fourth nerve
A nuclear fourth nerve lesion is contralateral to the palsy and often comes with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome (adjacent sympathetic fibers)

pitfalls: Skew deviation (a supranuclear vertical misalignment from brainstem or cerebellar lesions) mimics a fourth nerve palsy; it lacks excyclotorsion of the higher eye and changes with lying down

nuclei.component: GSE to the contralateral superior oblique

exit.brainstemExit: Dorsal midbrain below the inferior colliculus, after decussating in the superior medullary velum
exit.cisternalCourse: Around the cerebral peduncle in the ambient cistern under the free edge of the tentorium, between the PCA and SCA laterally
exit.foramen: Superior orbital fissure (outside the annulus of Zinn)
exit.extracranialCourse: Crosses over the levator and superior rectus to the superior oblique in the superomedial orbit

tests.name: Three-step test
tests.how: Identify the hypertropic eye, then whether it worsens on right or left gaze, then on right or left head tilt
tests.abnormal: Hypertropia worse on contralateral gaze and ipsilateral head tilt

tests.name: Down and in gaze
tests.how: Ask the patient to look down while adducting

tests.name: Torsion
tests.how: Double Maddox rod or fundus photography

lesionSigns.sign: Isolated superior oblique palsy after head injury
lesionSigns.localisingValue: peripheral nerve at the dorsal midbrain exit or along the tentorium

lesionSigns.sign: Palsy contralateral to a midbrain lesion
Palsy with III, VI and V1

lesionSigns.localisingValue: trauma at the decussation (superior medullary velum)

cranial.nuclearVsPeripheral: Because the fibers cross before leaving the brainstem, nuclear and fascicular lesions cause a palsy of the opposite eye, often with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome or a contralateral sensory loss from the adjacent tegmentum; peripheral lesions cause an ipsilateral palsy.
